TREASURER OF HER MAJESTY’S CHAMBER - WARRANT AND
RECKONING
Dated at Whitehall, xvto Marcij 1594 (15 March 1594/5)
Warrant of payment unto William Kempe, William Shakespeare, and Richard
Burbage, servants to the Lord Chamberlain, upon the Council’s warrant dated at
Whitehall the fifteenth day of March 1594, for two several comedies or
interludes showed by them before Her Majesty in Christmas time last past at
Greenwich, namely upon St Stephen’s Day (26 December) and Innocents’ Day (28
December).
Sum allowed by the Chamber:
- For the two comedies at Greenwich: 13 pounds, 6 shillings, 8 pence.
- By way of Her Majesty’s special reward: 6 pounds, 13 shillings, 4 pence.
- Total received in coin (sixteen angels, four sovereigns, and eight pounds
 in white money): 20 pounds.
Company disbursement cast by John Heminges at James Burbage’s house in
Holywell:
- Boat-hire to Greenwich and return across two days, with carriage of the
 costume baskets: 16 shillings.
- Rewards to five hired men at four shillings each, three boy players at two
 shillings each, and the book-keeper and tireman at four shillings each: 34
 shillings.
- Debt discharged to the mercer in Cheapside for cloth taken up before
 Christmas: 50 shillings.
- Remainder divided into eight equal parts (seven sharers and one part to
 the company stock): 15 pounds, being 37 shillings and 6 pence per part.
 Out of the stock part, 8 shillings set aside for Mistress Edith
 Kettlewood, payable Thursday.
Entered and acknowledged at Holywell, 15 March 1595. Acquittance sealed by
John Heminges on behalf of the fellowship.

## Page 1

MEMORANDUM OF LEASE HEADS - THE THEATRE GROUND,
HOLYWELL
Minutes brought from Cuthbert Burbage (10 May) and read at the Theatre, Monday
12 May 1595
Lessor: Giles Allen, gentleman, of Haseleigh in Essex. Lessee: James Burbage,
joiner and player, of Holywell, Shoreditch. Present term: twenty-one years
from 13 April 1576, expiring April 1597 (two years less a month remaining) at
the old reserved rent of 14 pounds by the year.
Heads demanded by Master Allen for any new covenant:
1. Annual Rent. The yearly rent for the parcel of ground, barns, and playhouse
yard to be raised from 14 pounds to 24 pounds per annum, payable at the four
usual quarter-days.
2. Repairs and Upkeep. Lessee to covenant to bear all charges upon the timber
frame, galleries, tiled roof, and boundary wall out of the company’s own
purse.
3. Clause Touching the House After Five Years. Master Allen demands a further
clause touching the playhouse itself after five years of any renewed term. He
has neither explained the words of this clause nor delivered a fair copy to be
read.
4. Timber Ownership. Under the original 1576 indenture, the playhouse frame
was erected at James Burbage’s own cost with covenant to take down and remove
the timber before expiry if no new term be sealed.
Minute entered at the Theatre, 12 May 1595:
Present: James Burbage, Richard Burbage, John Heminges, Thomas Pope, William
Shakespeare. No figure agreed, no term accepted, and no sum entered in the
company book. The five-year clause remains unread.

PETITION OF THE LORD MAYOR AND ALDERMEN OF LONDON TO
THE PRIVY COUNCIL
Guildhall copyist’s digest of the letter of 13 September 1595 (received in
Shoreditch, 15 September)
To the Right Honourable the Lords and others of Her Majesty’s Most Honourable
Privy Council. The humble suit of the Lord Mayor and Aldermen of the City of
London touching stage plays in the suburbs and liberties adjoining.
Heads reported from the Guildhall letter of 13 September:
1. Disorders and Resort. The petition names the Bankside playhouses, cites the
late June stirs and disorderly assemblies of apprentices, vagrants, and
masterless men, and prays letters to the Justices of Surrey and Middlesex.
Whether the Theatre in Shoreditch is named in so many words the Guildhall
copyist could not swear.
2. Contagion and Scarcity. The City pleads the dearness of corn and danger of
infection from crowds drawn out of the parishes into the liberties on working
afternoons.
3. Prayer for Restraint. The Aldermen pray the Council to grant letters of
restraint forbidding stage plays in and about the suburbs until the City’s
quiet be better assured.
Note endorsed at the Theatre, Monday 15 September 1595:
No Council order has come down. The afternoon bill for The Knave stood as
posted at two of the clock; the company awaits word from the Lord Chamberlain
before altering any playing day.
